claims.text: RENUMBERING AND ATTRITION BETWEEN COMMITTEE AND FLOOR. In S. 2103 as reported by the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence on 22 June 2023, Title XI--Other Matters contained four sections: 'Sec. 1101. Modification of reporting requirement for All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office.'; 'Sec. 1102. Modifications to notification on the provision of defense sensitive [support]'; 'Sec. 1103. Modification of congressional oversight of special access programs.'; and 'Sec. 1104. Funding limitations relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena.' The engrossed Division M carries only the first and the last of these, renumbered 1101 and 1102. Two provisions were therefore dropped between committee and the Senate-passed text, and one of the two dropped provisions was a direct amendment to the congressional oversight regime for special access programs. That is a soft joint the board did not previously have: the same intelligence committee that wrote the UAP funding limitation also wrote a special access program oversight amendment alongside it, and only the funding limitation survived to the floor text.

claims.source: Brandi Vincent, 'Senate's intelligence authorization bill questions reverse engineering of government-recovered UAPs', DefenseScoop, 27 June 2023 - https://defensescoop.com/2023/06/27/senates-intelligence-authorization-bill-questions-reverse-engineering-of-government-recovered-uaps/
claims.text: Because the engrossed body was never read, the specific elements the board attributes to Sec. 1102 - a 60-day contractor notification deadline running to the Director of AARO, a 180-day deadline to make material available, the phrase 'non-earth origin or exotic', and the phrase 'assessment, analysis, and inspection' - remain corroborated ONLY by DefenseScoop's 27 June 2023 report, and that report is describing Sec. 1104 of S. 2103 as reported, not Sec. 1102 of Division M as engrossed. The reporter quotes the following fragments inside quotation marks: a mandate on any person currently or formerly under contract with the federal government that 'has in their possession material or information provided by or derived from the' government relating to UAP 'that formerly or currently is protected by any form of special access or restricted access' to notify the AARO Director within 60 days of enactment; and, no later than 180 days after passage, to make 'all such material and information' and 'a comprehensive list of all non-earth origin or exotic [UAP] material' available to AARO for 'assessment, analysis, and inspection'. The bracketed [UAP] is the reporter's insertion, which is itself a sign that the quoted string is being edited. Treat these as reported fragments of the REPORTED text, not as verified text of the ENGROSSED section.

claims.text: ENACTED SUCCESSOR IDENTIFIED AND CONFIRMED FROM A PRIMARY SOURCE. The provision was enacted as Section 7343 of Division G of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2024, Pub. L. 118-31. The Explanatory Statement to accompany the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2024, printed in the Congressional Record by Sen. Warner on 14 December 2023 and given the same effect as a joint explanatory statement of a conference committee, states verbatim: 'Section 7343 of the Act provides for funding limitations relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena because of perceptions of insufficient transparency in this area. Section 7343 is also intended to avoid technology and security stovepipes and expand awareness regarding any historical exotic technology antecedents previously provided by the Federal Government for research and development purposes if they are shown to exist. Section 7343 further provides a limitation regarding independent research and development funding to ensure that certain indirect expenses are prohibited.' The explanatory statement says nothing whatever about a 60-day contractor turn-in, a list of non-earth origin material, or a make-available mandate to AARO.

Limitation on use of funds for certain unreported programs.' in Division A, Title XVI, distinct from and in addition to Sec. 7343 in Division G. claims.source: Office of the Law Revision Counsel, 50 U.S.C. 3373, statutory notes (text in effect on 20 August 2026) - https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title50-section3373&num=0&edition=prelim
claims.text: THE ONLY PART OF THE ENACTED FAMILY THAT COULD BE READ VERBATIM CONTAINS NONE OF THE THREE DISPUTED ELEMENTS. The Office of the Law Revision Counsel sets out subsections (b) and (c) of Pub. L. 118-31, div. A, title XVI, Sec. 1687 as a statutory note under 50 U.S.C. 3373, under the heading 'Limitation Regarding Independent Research and Development'. The full text of subsection (b) as set out reads: 'Consistent with Department of Defense Instruction Number 3204.01 (dated August 20, 2014, incorporating change 2, dated July 9, 2020; relating to Department policy for oversight of independent research and development), independent research and development funding relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena shall not be allowable as indirect expenses for purposes of contracts covered by such instruction, unless such material and information is made available the appropriate congressional committees and congressional leadership.' Subsection (c) then defines 'appropriate congressional committees' as the congressional defense committees plus the two intelligence committees, and 'congressional leadership' as the Senate majority and minority leaders and the Speaker and House minority leader. There is no 60-day deadline, no 180-day deadline, no 'non-earth origin or exotic' language, and no reference to AARO anywhere in the enacted text that OLRC chose to print. The sentence also carries a drafting error that survived into law - 'is made available the appropriate congressional committees', with the preposition 'to' missing - which is itself evidence that this is the enacted text and not a paraphrase. NOTE THE LIMIT OF THIS FINDING: it establishes what is in Sec. 1687(b)-(c), not what is in Sec. 7343, whose body was not retrieved. OLRC set out only subsections (b) and (c) of Sec. 1687 and set out no part of Sec. 7343 as a note anywhere the board has checked.

desc: Warner's Section 1102 is the most direct legislative assault on contractor-held material ever passed by a chamber of Congress, and it is far less well known than the eminent domain clause. It opens with a sense of Congress that the Federal Government 'must expand awareness about any historical exotic technology antecedents previously provided by the Federal Government for research and development purposes' — a statement that the Government has previously handed exotic technology to industry. It then cuts off all funds for UAP activity under special or restricted access not 'formally, officially, explicitly, and specifically described, explained, and justified' to Congress and the AARO Director, enumerating six categories including personnel whose mission is 'capturing, recovering, and securing unidentified anomalous phenomena craft or pieces and components of such craft,' analysis to determine 'material composition, method of manufacture, origin,' 'reverse engineering or replicating unidentified anomalous phenomena technology,' and 'any aerospace craft that uses propulsion technology other than chemical propellants, solar power, or electric ion thrust.' Subsection (d) then requires any current or former Federal contractor holding such material to notify the AARO Director within 60 days and, within 180 days, to make available all of it plus 'a comprehensive list of all non-earth origin or exotic unidentified anomalous phenomena material.' Subsection (e) grants full civil and criminal immunity to those who comply. Subsection (f) disallows independent research and development funding on such material as an indirect expense unless it is surrendered, effective 60 days after enactment and applicable to money appropriated before as well as after. The Senate passed all of this on 27 July 2023.

dossier.denialPosture: The executive branch answer to this provision was delivered in advance and in writing by Pentagon spokesperson Sue Gough, who stated on 5 June 2023 that "AARO has not discovered any verifiable information to substantiate claims that any programs regarding the possession or reverse-engineering of extraterrestrial materials have existed in the past or exist currently," and on 22 June 2023 that "AARO has been rigorously investigating alleged programs mentioned by individuals who have come forward as part of the congressionally-mandated historical review. To date, AARO has not been denied access to any United States government program, past or present, during the course of its work." Johnson noted that the second statement is carefully scoped: Grusch did not come forward as part of the historical review, so the sentence may not have covered his allegations at all.
dossier.narrative:
On 14 June 2023, nine days after The Debrief published David Grusch's allegations, the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence adopted by voice vote a UAP amendment sponsored by Senator Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY) and cosponsored by Senators Mike Rounds (R-SD), John Cornyn (R-TX) and Marco Rubio (R-FL). The committee then approved the underlying Intelligence Authorization Act unanimously. The bill was filed and numbered on 22 June 2023 as S. 2103; the UAP text appeared as Section 1104, titled "Funding limitations relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena." Section 1102 of that same reported text was an unrelated provision on defense sensitive support; the board's identifier tracks a later renumbering as the IAA moved into the NDAA vehicle, and the substance — not the number — is what matters.

The operative mechanism had three parts.

First, a notification and turn-in mandate. The text reached "any person currently or formerly under contract with the Federal Government that has in their possession material or information provided by or derived from the Federal Government relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena that formerly or currently is protected by any form of special access or restricted access." Such persons had 60 days from enactment to notify the AARO director, and 180 days to provide "a comprehensive list of all non-earth origin or exotic unidentified anomalous phenomena material" in their possession and to make it available to the director for "assessment, analysis, and inspection." The AARO director then had 30 days to notify designated congressional committees and leaders of any notification, information or material received. That last clause is the accountability trigger: it would have created a dated congressional paper trail for each turn-in.

Second, a safe harbor: "No criminal or civil action may lie or be maintained in any Federal or State court against any person for receiving" the covered material or information, contingent on meeting the deadlines. Douglas Johnson, who first reported the text, read this as implying that a private entity holding non-human technology outside democratic oversight — and possibly profiting from it — would otherwise be in a legally tenuous position, and that the provision functioned as a time-limited amnesty to smooth an orderly return. Nothing in the provision created new criminal offenses, and nothing immunized threats, violence or perjury.

Third, a funding ban. No future federal funds, directly or indirectly, for any UAP-related special access program activity unless the program had been "formally, officially, explicitly, and specifically described, explained, and justified to the appropriate committees of Congress, congressional leadership, and the Director" of AARO. The designated recipients were the intelligence, armed services and appropriations committees of both chambers plus the Speaker, House minority leader, and Senate majority and minority leaders — 58 senators and 137 House members in total. The categories of covered activity were drafted in six expansive paragraphs and included recruiting, employing, training, equipping, operating and providing security for government or contractor personnel with a retrieval mission; managing and providing security for activities and information relating to UAP "from disclosure"; and reverse-engineering work reaching any aerospace craft using propulsion other than chemical propellants, solar power and electric ion thrust.

The Sense of Congress attached to the provision is the most candid language Congress has produced on the subject. It asserted that "due to the increasing potential for technology surprise from foreign adversaries and to ensure sufficient integration across the United States industrial base and avoid technology and security stovepipes... the Federal Government must expand awareness about any historical exotic technology antecedents previously provided by the Federal Government for research and development purposes." Read plainly: the government previously provided exotic technology antecedents to industry for R&D, secrecy has stovepiped that work, and the stovepiping is now a national security liability. Whether or not one accepts the premise, the drafters wrote it into a bill that a Senate committee approved unanimously.

The legislative arc from there is the concealment story in miniature. The Senate Armed Services Committee carried parallel but non-identical language at Section 1546 of S. 2226, without the safe harbor and without the Sense of Congress, and with the funding limitation confined to FY2024 DoD programs. On 20 July 2023 SSCI Chairman Mark Warner filed a revised version, SA 994, narrowing the IAA's funding limitation to FY2024 as well. The House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence approved its own FY2024 IAA (H.R. 3932) on 13 July 2023 containing no UAP provisions at all, and the House Rules Committee blocked a floor vote on Rep. Mike Gallagher's parallel amendment to the House NDAA — reportedly because of objections from HPSCI leadership, whose chairman Michael Turner and ranking member Jim Himes had made dismissive public comments about secret alien technology on 6 June 2023. The Senate passed a combined NDAA-IAA on 27 July 2023. In conference, the turn-in mandate and safe harbor did not survive. What was enacted on 22 December 2023 as Section 7343 of Division G of P.L. 118-31 is a funding limitation only, conditioned on the Director of National Intelligence providing program details to the appropriate committees and leadership — which the Intelligence chairmen explained "provides for funding limitations relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena because of perceptions of insufficient transparency in this area."

The deletion is the finding. A unanimous committee wrote a hand-back-the-material provision with an amnesty clause, and the amnesty and the hand-back both vanished behind closed doors.
openQuestions: Exactly which section number the provision carried in the Senate-passed combined NDAA-IAA text (Division M, 27 July 2023) before final renumbering to Section 7343 of Division G.
Who in conference moved to strike the 60-day notification, the 180-day turn-in, and the safe harbor, and is there any written conference record of the objection?
Did any contractor make a voluntary notification to AARO under the spirit of the proposed provision, and did AARO log any such contact?
What did SSCI staff know, from classified sources, that led a unanimous committee to draft an amnesty for entities 'receiving' non-earth-origin material?
What became of the enacted Section 7343 funding limitation — did the DNI ever certify any program to the committees under it, and did it lapse after FY2024?

Which specific 'historical exotic technology antecedents previously provided by the Federal Government for research and development purposes' did the Sense of Congress have in mind, and who briefed the committee on them?
dossier.whatItIs: The contractor turn-in provision of the Fiscal Year 2024 Intelligence Authorization Act: a Gillibrand amendment adopted unanimously by the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence on 14 June 2023, which required any person currently or formerly under federal contract holding government-derived UAP material to notify AARO within 60 days and, within 180 days, to hand over "a comprehensive list of all non-earth origin or exotic unidentified anomalous phenomena material" for assessment, analysis and inspection. It carried a safe harbor, a sweeping funding ban on unreported UAP special access programs, and a Sense of Congress. It was numbered Sec. 1104 in S. 2103 as reported on 22 June 2023, renumbered as the bill moved, and was enacted in drastically narrowed form as Section 7343 of Division G of P.L. 118-31 on 22 December 2023.
dossier.whyImplicated: This is the single most important statutory hook on the board because it is the only text Congress has ever voted out of committee that presumes, on its face, that private contractors are holding non-earth-origin material derived from federal programs and that treats getting it back as an administrative problem with a deadline. A safe harbor is not written for a hypothetical. Congress does not draft immunity from criminal and civil action "for receiving" material unless someone plausibly received it. The definition of covered activities is equally load-bearing: it contemplates government or contractor personnel with "a primary, secondary, or contingency mission of capturing, recovering, and securing unidentified anomalous phenomena craft or pieces and components of such craft," and it defines the reverse-engineering perimeter as work on "any aerospace craft that uses propulsion technology other than chemical propellants, solar power, and electric ion thrust." Seventeen senators on the Intelligence Committee voted this text out. Then it was cut in conference.

entityInfo.desc:
Senate-passed IAA FY2024 Sec. 1102(d), verbatim:

'(d) Notification and Reporting.--Any person currently or formerly under contract with the Federal Government that has in their possession material or information provided by or derived from the Federal Government relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena that formerly or currently is protected by any form of special access or restricted access shall-- (1) not later than 60 days after the date of the enactment of this Act, notify the Director of such possession; and (2) not later than 180 days after the date of the enactment of this Act, make available to the Director for assessment, analysis, and inspection-- (A) all such material and information; and (B) a comprehensive list of all non-earth origin or exotic unidentified anomalous phenomena material.'

And Sec. 1102(e): 'No criminal or civil action may lie or be maintained in any Federal or State court against any person for receiving material or information described in subsection (d) if that person complies with the notification and reporting provisions described in such subsection.'

None of this appears in the enacted Sec. 7343 of P.L. 118-31.
